title: AI Content Moderation Platforms: The Invisible Editor
body:
Information flow in GLMZ is regulated at the infrastructure level through AI Content Moderation Platforms, systems that operate on every licensed communications network in the city. The dominant platform, FILTER-9, is jointly operated by the Municipal Communications Authority and a consortium of licensed network providers. FILTER-9 processes text, audio, image, and video content in near-real-time as it transits the network, classifying material against a continuously updated taxonomy of restricted categories. The taxonomy itself is not publicly released in full; the MCA publishes a summary document describing broad categories (incitement, infrastructure coordination, unlicensed financial solicitation) while the operational ruleset contains thousands of specific sub-classifications that are revised monthly without public notice.

FILTER-9's technical architecture relies on a multi-stage pipeline. A fast, lightweight classifier performs initial triage on all content, flagging a subset for deeper analysis by more computationally expensive models. Content flagged as high-confidence violations is automatically suppressed — the sender receives a delivery confirmation but the content does not reach its destination, a practice known colloquially as 'ghost blocking.' Content in uncertain classifications enters a human review queue, though budget constraints mean human reviewers address fewer than 12% of queued items within 24 hours; the remainder are resolved by a secondary automated arbitration model. Appeals are theoretically available through a web portal, but the appeals process requires identity verification that many Tier 4 and 5 residents are unwilling to provide given the surveillance implications.

The moderation taxonomy has been documented to suppress content that poses no credible harm but that carries political or economic inconvenience for licensed network operators and their corporate partners. Labor organizing communications, documentation of infrastructure failures in low-tier districts, and reporting on corporate misconduct regularly trigger suppression under the 'infrastructure coordination' and 'unlicensed financial solicitation' sub-classifications. Researchers at the Meridian Press Freedom Collective have built a shadow monitoring system that compares content sent on licensed networks with content simultaneously broadcast on unlicensed mesh networks, cataloguing systematic suppression patterns that FILTER-9's operators deny exist.

Tier 1 and 2 corporate users access the network through exemption channels — high-bandwidth enterprise tiers that carry reduced moderation intensity and that grant corporate communications teams the ability to whitelist specific content categories for internal distribution. This creates an asymmetric information environment in which upper-tier actors can discuss topics that would be automatically suppressed if the same content traveled through standard consumer network tiers. Investigative journalists have documented cases in which corporate communications explicitly referencing regulatory violations traveled freely on enterprise exemption channels while citizen reporting on the same violations was suppressed on consumer networks within minutes of transmission.
